title: Spectral-temporal patterns of vegetation communities: Identifying where and when biological information emerges in imaging spectroscopy data
abstract: Imaging spectroscopy provides detailed insights into terrestrial ecosystem physiology and biodiversity, and recent missions are expanding its operational scope. Key challenges remain, however, in interpreting the information contained in reflectance spectra and optimizing their use for vegetation monitoring. Here we ask ( Obj1 ) where along the spectrum and ( Obj2 ) when during the phenological cycle is vegetation class-discriminative spectral information most strongly expressed? We analyzed data from the NASA Surface Biology and Geology High-Frequency Time Series (SHIFT) campaign, covering eight vegetation communities across three plant functional types in a coastal Mediterranean ecosystem. To address both objectives, we combined three conceptually independent approaches that characterize spectral shape divergence, characteristic local structure, and class separability. By identifying spectral regions highlighted consistently across methods, we localized informative segments of the spectrum and tracked how their importance evolved through time. We further evaluated the operational implications of reduced temporal sampling through time-ablation experiments controlling for both the number of acquisition dates and revisit frequency. Results revealed community-specific regions of enhanced information content together with distinct periods of maximum discriminability. Mapping accuracy remained robust under reduced sampling, retaining 94.8% of optimal performance when revisit intervals increased from one to two weeks, and 91.3% for monthly cloud-free acquisitions. Vegetation discriminability was both spectrally localized and temporally dynamic, indicating that spectral and temporal dimensions are best considered jointly. These findings suggest that incorporating phenological and environmental gradients into sampling strategies may improve the scientific return of future environmental imaging spectroscopy missions.

title: Global 30 m forest canopy height mapping through harmonized GEDI and ICESat-2 LiDAR integration with multi-source images
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Accurate and spatially explicit forest canopy height (FCH) estimates are essential for biomass estimation, carbon accounting, and ecosystem assessment at global scales. Nevertheless, generating a coherent high-resolution global FCH product remains challenging due to cross-sensor inconsistencies among spaceborne LiDAR missions, pronounced ecological heterogeneity, and highly uneven sampling density. This study presents a global 30 m FCH map for 2020 derived from harmonized GEDI and ICESat-2 observations integrated with Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical imagery, and ancillary environmental datasets. A regression-based cross-sensor calibration model was developed to align ICESat-2 canopy height metrics with the GEDI reference scale, producing a unified LiDAR training dataset and extending structurally consistent information into high-latitude regions beyond GEDI coverage. Cross-sensor harmonization enabled GEDI and ICESat-2 samples to be consistently pooled into an expanded training dataset, yielding better mapping performance than unharmonized pooling. To account for spatial heterogeneity and sampling imbalance, we implemented an adaptive quad-tree regionalization scheme driven by LiDAR sample density. This approach enhances model stability in data-rich regions while avoiding unnecessary subdivision in data-sparse areas. Regional FCH estimation was performed using a hybrid Random Forest-Ordinary Kriging (RFOK) framework that integrates nonlinear regression with spatially structured residual interpolation. Compared with regression-only models, RFOK increased R 2 from 0.65 to 0.72 and reduced RMSE by 11.39% under withheld 10% spaceborne LiDAR validation samples, with an additional 9.16% reduction in RMSE against independent airborne LiDAR data. Accuracy validation of the global FCH map using withheld spaceborne LiDAR samples and independent airborne LiDAR datasets demonstrates strong agreement, yielding R 2 = 0.72 (RMSE = 4.98 m; bias = 0.34 m) and R 2 = 0.70 (RMSE = 5.06 m; bias = −0.06 m), respectively. Within the evaluated validation framework, comparisons with the Potapov and Lang products indicate improved agreement with independent LiDAR reference data, including in high-latitude regions beyond GEDI coverage. The resulting 30 m global FCH map provides a spatially coherent and sensor-consistent representation of forest vertical structure, offering a robust data foundation for biomass estimation, carbon cycle assessment, and ecosystem monitoring.
